meta.title: Who really said "Democracy is the worst form of government except all those others"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Churchill really did say it — House of Commons, 11 November 1947 — but he introduced it with 'it has been said,' explicitly flagging it as an existing saying. He is the populariser, not the author. The originator is unknown.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Democracy is the worst form of government except all those others'?
meta.ogDescription: Churchill said it in the Commons in 1947 — but prefaced it with 'it has been said.' He was quoting, and he told us so. The real originator has never been identified.

answer.label: Churchill said it — but told the House he was quoting someone else
answer.authorDates: 1874–1965 · British prime minister and Nobel laureate
answer.sourceLine: He said it in the House of Commons on 11 November 1947, and Hansard records the words exactly. But the sentence begins “Indeed, it has been said that…” — Churchill was explicitly passing on an existing saying, not claiming one. Strip those four words, as almost every reproduction does, and you convert an honest attribution into a false one.

docMeta.dd: Parliament Bill debate, House of Commons

source.excerpt: No one pretends that democracy is perfect or all-wise. Indeed, it has been said that democracy is the worst form of Government except all those other forms that have been tried from time to time.
trail: Hansard records the words in the Parliament Bill debate of 11 November 1947 — including the crucial opening clause, ‘Indeed, it has been said that…’ Hansard, HC Deb 11 Nov 1947 ↗.

The saying was already in circulation before he used it. The closest earlier match found is a May 1946 Nova Scotia report on adult education — ‘it has even been called the worst form of government, except for all others which have been tried’ — whose author also disclaimed credit, so it was current before mid-1946 Quote Investigator ↗.

The International Churchill Society and his estate’s own editor credit him as the populariser of an unsourced aphorism rather than its author — the same conclusion he stated himself in the chamber International Churchill Society ↗.
source.excerptNote: The passage as Hansard records it. Note both the preceding sentence and the ‘it has been said’ clause — together they show a man carefully not claiming authorship.

Churchill died on 24 January 1965, so his speeches remain protected in the UK and EU until the end of 2035, and the literary estate’s permissions are actively administered by Curtis Brown. Practically: quoting this one sentence in a talk, an article or a book, with attribution, is ordinary quotation practice and is not something anyone seeks a licence for. Reproducing long passages of the speech, or putting the line on merchandise, is a different matter — commercial decorative use is licensed and enforced, and using his name to sell goods raises estate and brand issues separate from copyright. author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British prime minister, statesman & Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: Sir Winston Churchill led Britain through the Second World War and won the 1953 Nobel Prize in Literature. He spoke these words in opposition in 1947, arguing against curtailing the House of Lords’ powers. He was a careful attributor when he chose to be — which is what makes this case unusual: the man most burdened with invented quotations is here being credited with one he openly said was not his.

misattribution.heading: He said it — he just didn't claim it
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake quotation. Churchill said these words, on a known date, recorded in Hansard. The problem is subtler and more interesting: the four words that are always cut are the ones in which he tells you he is quoting someone else.

items.why: Hansard has ‘Indeed, it has been said that democracy is the worst form of Government…’ Virtually every reproduction drops the opening, turning a quotation-within-a-speech into an original epigram Hansard ↗.

The saying was already circulating by mid-1946, and the earliest close match found — a Nova Scotia education report — also disclaimed credit. Thematic precursors exist from the 1890s onward, but nobody has produced the author the search ↗.
Hansard reads ‘except all those other forms’ — no ‘for.’ The ubiquitous modern version adds it, and shorter paraphrases (‘except for all the others’) drift further still.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely spoken by Churchill in the Commons on 11 November 1947 — but prefaced ‘it has been said,’ so he is the populariser, not the author. The originator remains unknown Churchill Society ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: He was speaking in opposition, resisting a bill to curtail the power of the House of Lords, and the line is a defence of imperfect institutions against confident reformers. Read whole, the passage is less a witticism than a warning about tinkering with checks you did not build.
It has since become the standard sentence for defending democracy at its least impressive — which is a fair use of it, and one Churchill would probably have enjoyed, having borrowed it himself.
detailsBody: Preceding sentence: ‘No one pretends that democracy is perfect or all-wise.’
As recorded: ‘Indeed, it has been said that democracy is the worst form of Government except all those other forms that have been tried from time to time.’
Earliest close match: a May 1946 Nova Scotia report — whose author also disclaimed credit.
Modern form: the opening clause dropped, and ‘for’ inserted before ‘all those other forms.’
context.pull: The four words always cut are the ones where he says it isn't his.
